name: Halftone
basis: why: a press lays ink or nothing, so grey is faked with dots; how: rotated lattice, dot area by tone, CMYK at four angles

lumenary.blurb: Print-shop dots: one ink, four inks, or colour on black.

why: A press can lay down ink or leave paper bare, nothing in between, so printers fake grey with dots: small for light, large for dark. Your eye blends them when they are small enough. Colour printing repeats that with four inks, each on its own lattice turned to a different angle, so the dots interleave in a neat rosette instead of fighting each other.
how: Rotate a square lattice by the screen angle and lay it over the picture.
Sample the picture at each lattice point.
Draw a circle whose area is proportional to the ink that tone needs, so the radius is the square root of the tone.
In four colour mode, separate the picture into cyan, magenta, yellow and black and draw four lattices at 15, 75, 0 and 45 degrees with the multiply blend.
In colour on black mode, let dots grow with brightness and take the cell’s colour.
history: Stephen Horgan printed the first halftone photograph in a daily newspaper in 1880, and Frederic Ives patented a halftone process in 1881. Four colour offset printing through the twentieth century made the dot the basis of nearly every magazine, and it is why a close look at a printed photograph shows rosettes.
terms: The angle at which a dot lattice is rotated.
A wavy interference pattern made when two regular grids overlap at nearly the same angle.
Cyan, magenta, yellow and black: the four inks of most colour printing.
paragraphs: Printing cannot make grey, only ink or no ink, so a printer fakes tone with dots of varying size arranged on a regular lattice. The same trick is done here. A square lattice with spacing s is rotated by the screen angle and laid over the picture; at every lattice point the picture is sampled and a circle is drawn whose area is proportional to how much ink that tone needs. Area grows with the square of the radius, so the radius is the square root of the tone.

In four-colour mode the picture is separated into cyan, magenta, yellow and black the way a print shop does, and four lattices are drawn with the “multiply” blend so the inks combine like transparent printing inks. The four lattices use the traditional screen angles of 15°, 75°, 0° and 45° (shifted together by the angle slider), because overlaying grids at the same angle causes visible moiré while grids at well-separated angles produce the small rosette pattern seen in magazines. “Color on black” turns it around: dots grow with brightness and take the cell’s colour, normalised so the strongest channel is full.

equations.note: Dot centres on a lattice of spacing s rotated by θ about the picture centre c.
Radius of a one-ink dot; g is dot gain and adj() the contrast curve.
RGB to CMYK separation (channels in 0 to 1).

presets.text: Four colour mode with large dots shows the printing process itself.
Fine dots at 45 degrees are close to a photograph.
Colour on black glows like a lit billboard.
